Before drawing conclusions, the researchers checked their measured subgroup against the full half-million-person cohort across age, sex, body size, deprivation and more, confirmed the randomly selected portion mirrored the whole population, and then deliberately ran their main genetic-discovery analyses on that representative subgroup so the findings would generalize.

Before drawing conclusions, the team checked that their measurements held steady: the same protein measured on different panels agreed, repeat samples gave near-identical readings, and—crucially—they split their data and confirmed the genetic links found in one half reappeared in a separate replication group with almost perfectly matching strengths. A concrete look at how a huge measurement effort proves its own readings are tight and repeatable.

When tallying the new brain cells that told them whether their treatment worked, the people doing the counting were kept unaware of which animals had received the drug and which the placebo — so their counts couldn't be nudged by what they hoped to find.

To judge how each mouse searched, the team didn't eyeball the swim paths — they wrote a rule-based program that applied the exact same numerical criteria to every single trial, sorting overlapping patterns in a fixed order and checking it on over 4,000 example trials (>90% agreement). In their discussion the authors repeatedly flag the limits of their own claims — admitting they 'cannot completely rule out' side effects on executive control, that a key link 'needs to be clarified in further studies,' and that the experiment's timing was 'too low' to test one rival explanation — a concrete look at attaching honest qualifiers to one's own findings.

To make sure their two-group split wasn't an accident of one dataset, the researchers repeatedly carved their sample into separate training and validation halves and checked that the same grouping reappeared each time — then confirmed it held up in a fully held-out batch of children, reproducing 89% of the time.
